This is a first draft:

The proposal introduces STARC-9, a large-scale, balanced dataset comprising 630,000 histopathology image tiles across nine colorectal cancer tissue classes. It also introduces DeepCluster++, a semi-automated pipeline for dataset construction that combines autoencoder-based feature extraction and clustering with pathologist verification. Visual inspection as a quality control measure significantly reduces manual effort, such as pathologist delineation of regions of interest within a whole slide image (WSI).
DeepCluster++ uses an autoencoder to capture fine-grained patterns, discover unlabeled clusters, and perform stratified, neighborhood-aware sampling to represent common and rare morphologies. This ensures that rare morphological patterns are represented alongside common ones, yielding a large, statistically balanced, nine-class dataset without excessive manual effort.
Together, these contributions aim to address the limitations of existing datasets, such as class imbalance and limited morphological diversity, while reducing the burden of manual annotation. The authors provide experimental evidence showing that models trained on STARC-9 achieve higher accuracy and generalizability than established benchmarks. They also make the dataset and code publicly available to promote reproducibility.  The datasets (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Path2AI/STARC-9/tree/main) and the weights corresponding to the models used in the empirical evaluation are available through the Huggingface platform. Additionally, the code corresponding to the DeepCluster++ methodology, as well as the code to train and evaluate the models, can be found in the provided GitHub repository.

A board-certified pathologist reviewed all 630,000 images for classification accuracy.


Limitations:

The methodology behind DeepCluster++ could be more detailed. There should be a rationale for design choices, such as feature extraction strategies, clustering parameters, and the use of autoencoders instead of more recent pathology foundation models.
Some potential biases are inadequately reported and may raise questions about representativeness, though this is not obvious at the tissue level.
Cross-center validation would have been useful for assessing generalizability of performance.
The evaluation strategy relies heavily on validation sets from the same center, lacking a thorough analysis of generalization across independent datasets. However, such datasets are scarce, and an additional evaluation using a public dataset corroborates the findings.
 

We propose accepting this presentation on the condition that the agreed-upon corrections are applied.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Thank you for your careful review and helpful recommendations. We have now added additional details regarding patient demographics to the revised version of the manuscript.

To summarize, for the 200 CRC WSI represented in STARC-9, 53% of the patients were male and 48% were female. The racial/ethnic distribution was: 64.5% White, 14% Hispanic, 12.5% Asian/Pacific Islander, 3.5% Black, and 5.5% Other/Unknown. Patients ranged in age from 23 to 97 years at the time of surgical resection, with a mean age of 62.9 years and a standard deviation of 16 years. The tumor grade distribution was as follows: 13% Grade 1 (n=26 WSI), 65% Grade 2 (n=130 WSI), 20% Grade 3 (n=40 WSI), and 2% Grade Not Applicable (n=4 WSI, all representing medullary carcinomas, for which standard grading is not applicable per current guidelines). With regard to histologic subtypes, 88.5% (n=177 WSI) were classified as Adenocarcinoma, 6.5% (n=13 WSI) were classified as Mucinous Adenocarcinoma, 2% (n=4 WSI) were classified as Medullary Carcinoma, 1.5% (n=3 WSI) were classified as Signet-ring Cell Carcinoma, and 1.5% (n=3 WSI) were classified as Carcinoma, Type Undetermined. With regard to microsatellite instability/DNA mismatch repair status, 56% (n=112 WSI) were from microsatellite stable (MSS) tumors and 9% (n=18 WSI) were from microsatellite unstable (MSI) tumors, with the remaining 35% from tumors on which MSI testing had not been performed. The relative representation of tumor locations was as follows: 43% (n=86 WSI) from the right or transverse colon, 28% (n=56 WSI) from the left colon, splenic flexure, or rectosigmoid colon, and 29% (n=58 WSI) from the rectum.

We have now also discussed the single-institutional nature and demographic distribution of our cohort with regard to potential bias as a limitation in the discussion section of the final manuscript and will also emphasize the need for future dataset extensions to address diversity and ensure fairness in downstream models trained on the dataset.

__1.Why the existing methodologies are not enough to build the STARC-9 dataset.__\
We thank the reviewer and have added a discussion of alternative methods to Section 2 of our revised manuscript. We now briefly survey three broad classes of dataset‐construction methodologies and explain why they fall short of our goal: 
* Manual annotation (e.g., using QuPath [13]): Gold-standard ROI delineation is prohibitively slow, subjective, and biased toward “easy” regions, making it difficult to capture rare morphologies (e.g., ADI, MUS) or maintain class balance as WSI size and complexity increase [39], [40].
* Random sampling: Fails to capture rare but important morphologies due to sampling error, creating an unbalanced representation of tissue heterogeneity across WSI’s.
* Deep clustering (e.g., K‑means on transfer‑learned features [19]): These methods automate cluster formation, but by sampling only around each cluster centroid, they bias selection toward the most common tissue morphologies and ignore the full spectrum of intra‑class variability needed for robust supervised learning. (In pathology‑specific variants of deep clustering [38], only up to 256 patches were sampled from each WSI after the application of K-means clustering.) 

Active learning [41] improves diversity by focusing on model-challenging samples but depends on iterative labeling and pre-existing labeled pools, which are scarce in histopathology. In contrast, DeepCluster++ uses an autoencoder to capture fine‐grained patterns, discovers clusters without labels, and performs stratified, neighborhood‐aware sampling to represent both common and rare morphologies without excessive manual effort. This ensures that rare morphological patterns are represented alongside common ones, yielding a large, statistically balanced 9 class dataset without excessive manual effort. \
[39] Pataki et al. HunCRC: annotated pathological slides to enhance deep learning applications in colorectal cancer screening. Sci Data 9, 370 (2022).\
[40] Koziarski et al. DiagSet: a dataset for prostate cancer histopathological image classification. Sci Rep 14, 6780 (2024). \
[41] Li, X et al. Unlabeled data selection for active learning in image classification. Sci Rep 14, 424 (2024). 

__2.I suggest performing targeted ablations on a smaller-scale subset, so that the importance of each component is clarified.__\
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive feedback. We carried out a targeted ablation on 10 randomly selected WSIs (independent of training/validation) for TUM and NCS classes:
* Samples per cluster (m): Tested m = 100 to 800. Small m (≈100) yields many tiny, redundant clusters; large m (≥ 800) mixes tissue types. m ≈ 400 balances intra-cluster purity and inter-cluster diversity.
* The number of bins was set to g=5 to capture the full morphological spectrum from "prototypical" (near-centroid) to "atypical" (edge-of-cluster). This ensures sampling of prognostically vital but rare interface patterns, such as tumor at the invasive front. We found g=5 was an optimal trade-off, as fewer bins merged distinct patterns, while more bins fragmented the sample space without adding meaningful distinction. 
* Sampling percentage (20%): By drawing an equal 20% of tiles from each of the five bins, we ensured uniform representation across the morphological continuum. This choice follows directly from g=5, providing a straightforward and reproducible sampling scheme. Adjusting the sampling percentage, it is possible to increase or decrease the size of the dataset. 

The Table 4 below shows the trade-off between cluster size (m) and purity (inverse of Shannon Entropy). As m increases, purity decreases (entropy rises). We selected m=400 as it provides substantial morphological variation while maintaining low tissue-type admixture, representing the best balance for our goal. 

Table 4. Cluster quality analysis.
| m   | Average Entropy | Morphologic Variation                   |
|-----|-----------------|------------------------------------------|
| 200 | 0.12 | Low |
| 400 | 0.41 | High |
| 600 | 1.73  | High (but mixed tissue types)            |
| 800 | 2.17 | High (but highly mixed tissue types)     |

__3.Why was an autoencoder chosen for feature extraction?__\
We chose a custom‑trained autoencoder (AE_CRC) over off‑the‑shelf pathology foundation models for three main reasons:
* Task-specific features: Foundation models are typically trained with classification or contrastive losses, which optimize their latent spaces to distinguish between major diagnostic categories. Such discriminative objectives may fail to capture the subtle, intra‑class feature variations important for representation of the full morphologic spectrum of tissue types, making it difficult to accurately distinguish differences between morphologically similar "edge cases" from two different tissue types, such as MUC and ADI. In contrast, AE_CRC is trained with a structural similarity loss, forcing it to reconstruct texture, contrast, and architectural details. This reconstruction objective yields a latent space ideally suited for morphology‑based clustering.
* Domain‑specific sensitivity: By training exclusively on over 100,000 CRC tiles, AE_CRC becomes finely attuned to colorectal (and other tubular gastrointestinal tract) histopathology. It learns to distinguish the fine-grained features present within tissue types such as NOR, MUC, TUM, and NCS. This is in contrast to existing pathology foundation models, which are trained on a wide variety of organs and tasks, causing these models to overlook the specific fine-grained features necessary for accurate representation within the latent space. 
* Efficiency and scalability: Large foundation models (e.g., CTransPath, UNI, CONCH) require substantial GPU resources and incur slower embedding times. AE_CRC, in contrast, is lightweight and fast to implement on standard hardware, making it practical for clustering 630,000 tiles in DeepCluster++ without incurring prohibitive compute costs.

In our experiments, clustering using AE_CRC embeddings yielded more coherent, morphology‑driven groups than either models trained on real images (like ImageNet) or contrastive learning-based pathology image encoders, enabling DeepCluster++ to sample both prototypical and edge‑case tiles effectively. This reconstruction‑based approach is therefore better aligned with the goal of building a large‑scale, diverse histopathology benchmark dataset. \
\
__4.How to choose the different hyperparameters?__\
Please refer to our reply to Comment #2 above for these details. \
\
__5.Formatting errors.__\
Thank you for catching these. We have corrected these in the final version of the manuscript.\
\
__6.Lack of clarity in tables.__ 
* __6.1 In Table 1, the meaning of the text in bold is not explained.__\
Thank you for pointing out this important oversight on our part. In Table 1, the highest‑accuracy models for each dataset (ViT‑Base on NCT, HiPT on HMU, and CTransPath on STARC‑9), are highlighted in bold. We have added this to the table footnote in the final version of the manuscript.    
__6.2 In Table 2, it is unclear whether the results correspond to the same model.__\
We apologize for the lack of clarity. The 2nd through 4th rows of Table 2 report the precision, recall, F1‑macro, and accuracy metrics for each of the three top‑performing models (with respect to accuracy) in Table 1 (e.g., the ones with the bold-faced model accuracies in Table 1), when validated on each of the three validation datasets (STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-SMALL, STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-LARGE, and CURATED-TCGA-CRC-HE-VAL-20K). These top-performing models were: ViT‑Base trained on NCT (abbreviated in Table 2 as "NCT"), HiPT trained on HMU (abbreviated in Table 2 as "HMU"), and CTransPath trained on STARC‑9 (abbreviated in Table 2 as "STARC-9"). The data in row 3 of Table 2 (validation results on STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-LARGE) correspond to the data in Table 1 for each row containing the bold-faced model accuracies in Table 1. We have added this information to the table footnote in the final version of the manuscript.   

__7.Bias and fairness. The paper does not discuss patient demographics.__\
We have now added additional details regarding patient demographics to the final version of the manuscript. In summary, for the STARC-9 dataset, 53% of patients were male and 48% female, with racial/ethnic distribution 64.5% White, 14% Hispanic, 12.5% Asian/Pacific Islander, 3.5% Black, and 5.5% Other/Unknown. Age range: 23-97 yrs (mean 62.9 yrs, standard deviation 16 yrs). We have also added discussion of demographics and potential bias in the limitations section of the revised manuscript.\
\
__8.Ethical Comments: The paper does not discuss patient demographics.__\
This has now been addressed in our reply to Comment #7 above.

We acknowledge the potential for bias in this setting. Therefore, we included an independent external validation set (TCGA-CRC, the only public CRC WSI dataset with full-thickness tissue sections available to us), for which results are presented in sections 4.1 and 4.2 (please see also Table 2).\
To further evaluate the generalizability of the model trained on STARC-9 in response to the reviewers’ comments, we curated a small test set of the seven common tissue classes taken from 10 WSI from the IMP‑CRS10K biopsy/polypectomy dataset [42]. In total, 1,093 image tiles were annotated for model performance validation, with results presented in Table 3 below. Re: use of the held-out validation datasets from our center, these were the only practical option available to us at the time, given the scarcity of publicly available CRC benchmark datasets containing the precise tissue type classes and pathologist-validated annotations required for external validation. Re: potential bias stemming from underrepresentation of specific minority racial/ethnic groups within our patient population, we have included additional discussion of this in the limitations section of the final manuscript.\
\
[42] Neto, P. C., et al. (2024). IMP Whole-Slide Images of Colorectal Samples 2024. INESC TEC.\
\
__3.The limitations of the paper are barely discussed.__\
While responding to the thoughtful questions posed by all of the reviewers, we added additional limitations, summarized below, which will be incorporated into the final manuscript:\
While STARC-9 contains extensive CRC tissue diversity across 9 tissue types, these may not exhaustively cover all potential tissue types to be found in CRC resections; future work might focus on incorporating additional, more granular tissue classes, as well as expanding the dataset for multi-modal applications through the addition of large-scale image-caption pairs. Additionally, as STARC-9 is limited to CRC patients, its relevance for model training/validation for other cancer types not sharing similar tumor morphologies or background non-tumor tissue classes (for example, central nervous system tumors) remains to be explored.   \
Lastly, as the patients represented in STARC-9 reflect the demographics of our geographic catchment area, some races/ethnicities (such as Black and Native American patients) may be relatively underrepresented. However, we have not found evidence in the literature to suggest that race/ethnicity impacts the histomorphology of tissue classes in CRC, so it is unclear whether imbalance in racial/ethnic representation would necessarily lead to bias in tissue type classification and segmentation-based models trained on STARC-9. We do acknowledge that race/ethnicity may impact clinical outcomes such as patient survival, so it will be important to include broader representation of all racial/ethnic groups in datasets used for the development of outcome prognostication models.\
\
__4.It would be interesting to mention the distribution of patients in the final version of STARC-9 (among the 200 initially planned). Is the number of tiles per patient balanced?__\
Re: patient distribution, please refer to our reply to Comment #1 above. Re: whether the number of tiles per patient was balanced, as WSI naturally vary in the amount and composition of tissue present on a slide, the per‑patient and even per‑tissue class tile counts were inherently imbalanced (for example, WSI with a high tumor volume tended to contain more NCS and MUC tiles). As this imbalanced tile distribution reflects the naturally diverse/heterogeneous tissue-type class distribution, it would be infeasible to balance the number of tiles of each tissue class per patient without running into the issues of (1) having an insufficient number of tiles from some patients and (2) needing to discard valid/informative tiles from some patients. Therefore, we did not seek to balance the number of tiles per patient.\
\
__5.It is unclear whether the WSIs used to train the AutoEncoder are the same as the tiles ultimately used in STARC-9. If so, doesn't this introduce bias? Especially since the features considered for clustering come from a CNN, doesn't this bias the analysis of various state-of-the-art methods (including CNNs)?__\
There was no patient overlap between the dataset used for autoencoder (AE_CRC) training and that used to construct the STARC‑9 training or validation sets. As our goal was to ensure that the autoencoder learned a robust, task‑agnostic representation of diverse histological patterns, we rigorously evaluated AE_CRC’s reconstruction performance across all nine tissue classes and observed that it achieved uniformly high SSIM and PSNR scores before deployment. In Phase 2 of our pipeline, we used only the frozen encoder of AE_CRC to generate unsupervised embeddings for clustering candidate image patches. These embeddings served solely to guide morphology‑aware tile sampling; they were not fed into any downstream classification or segmentation applications. All subsequent benchmark evaluations, whether using ResNet50, EfficientNetB7, ViT‑base, or other architectures, utilized raw tile images or features learned independently by each model backbone, thereby preventing any bias introduced by the AE_CRC.\
\
__6.In Section 3.3, it is unclear how tissue classes are identified and associated with tiles? The autoencoder is unsupervised.__\
As you noted, DeepCluster++ operates in an unsupervised fashion, so its output clusters do not carry semantic labels (e.g., “TUM” or “LYM”). We manually reviewed each output cluster to identify which tissue type it best fell into. To associate clusters with particular tissue types, once a cluster was labeled (for example, cluster_48 was confirmed as “TUM”), we used the embedding space proximity to find adjacent clusters, such as 2, 97, 53, and 112, sharing similar feature representations. In our experiments, these neighboring clusters consistently contained the same tissue morphology, allowing us to extend the “TUM” label across additional clusters with minimal additional time and effort. By iterating through this process (labeling a seed cluster and propagating its label to nearby clusters), we efficiently mapped appropriate clusters to the nine target tissue classes with only modest manual effort.\
\
__7.Since the validation sets come from the same center, do they include the same patients?__\
To ensure fair evaluation, the two center-specific validation sets (STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-SMALL from 20 WSI and STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-LARGE from 50 WSI) came from different patients. There was also no patient overlap with the WSI used in STARC‑9. (We also utilized an independent external validation TCGA-CRC dataset in our comparison of model performance.) \
\
__8.The authors observe a real performance gain on their validation sets when trained on STARC-9 compared to NCT and HMU. I wonder if the fact that the datasets come from the same center does not partly explain such a difference? It could be interesting to evaluate the performance of the models trained on STARC-9 and evaluated on NCT and HMU, in order to analyze the generalizability.__\
We agree that cross‐center validation would indeed be the gold standard for assessing performance generalizability. However, as noted in Section 2 (and in reference [11]), cross-center validation on the NCT and HMU datasets was not practically feasible in this case, as the original WSI used to generate these tile-level datasets were not publicly available for tissue-type label verification and refinement. Despite this limitation, we were able to observe higher performance of models trained on STARC-9 compared to those trained on NCT and HMU when validated on the independent external TCGA-CRC dataset, suggesting that the improvement in performance with STARC-9 on the validation datasets from our center were not entirely attributable to center-specific effects.

**1.The use of unsupervised autoencoders in DeepCluster++ to extract latent features for clustering is an interesting approach, but it raises concerns about whether the autoencoder can accurately capture image-level semantic information, which is crucial for precise dataset construction. If the feature embedding learned by the autoencoder is inaccurate, it will significantly impact the subsequent steps and affect the reliability of the dataset. The authors should conduct further analysis, such as statistical analysis and visualization, to address this concern.** \
Thank you for bringing up this important point. To encourage the AutoEncoder to focus on higher/image-level histological structural/morphologic patterns within the tissue types rather than low‑level pixel statistics, we trained it using a structural similarity loss. Compared to an AutoEncoder trained with simple MSE loss, using a Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss yielded markedly better reconstruction fidelity on the validation set STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-SMALL. The evaluation metrics showed lower pixel error (0.0012 vs 0.0015), higher SSIM (0.9262 vs 0.8863), and greater PSNR (32.48 dB vs 28.53 dB), which confirmed high‐fidelity reconstructions of complex tissue types such as NCS, TUM, etc., as shown in Figure 2(a). SSIM loss explicitly optimizes for texture, contrast, and spatial structure, encouraging the encoder to capture perceptually relevant features rather than minimizing average squared intensity differences. As a result, the latent space captures fine‑grained morphologic patterns across tissue types, collectively leading to more distinct and coherent clusters in DeepCluster++. In contrast, MSE‑trained models may blur subtle tissue variations, undermining cluster purity. The reconstruction quality indicates that the AutoEncoder-based feature extractor performed better than task-specific and contrastive learning-based encoders for clustering the various tissue types. \
\
**2.The statement "Finally, the selected tiles are verified by expert gastrointestinal pathologists to ensure classification accuracy" raises questions about whether all 630,000 images were reviewed by experts. If only a few samples are reviewed, this could be problematic in the medical field, as incorrect data can lead to biased models that affect clinical use. Additionally, the authors should provide information about the qualifications and experience of the pathologists involved in the review process to ensure the dataset's review process is reliable.**  \
Thank you for bringing up this important point. All 630,000 images were reviewed for classification accuracy by a board-certified pathologist with subspecialty expertise in GI pathology. Specifically, a total of three board-certified GI pathologists were involved in reviewing the images, with two of the pathologists (13 and 41 years of experience, respectively) reviewing subsets of the full dataset and the third pathologist (15 years of experience) performing final review of the full dataset (630,000 images).    \
\
**3.The performance of different models on the STARC-9 training set is surprisingly high, with even a simple ConvNet trained from scratch achieving an F1 score of 97.93 in Table 1. Given the large size of the training dataset, this raises concerns about the dataset's distribution and potential leakage of the STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL dataset into the training data. I suggest using some public validation sets to mitigate this concern.**  
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding potential data leakage. To clarify, our institutional training (STARC‑9) and validation (STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-SMALL and STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL-LARGE) datasets were drawn from different patients, with no overlap between any of the datasets.   \
We believe that the observed high classification accuracy, even for a ConvNet trained from scratch, is due to STARC‑9’s morphologic diversity across various tissue types. This breadth reduces overfitting risk and allows even simple architectures to learn robust discriminative features. As noted in our reply to Comment #8 raised by another reviewer (Reviewer bgDg), we agree that cross‐center validation using the other publicly available datasets (NCT and HMU) would indeed be ideal for assessing performance generalizability. To provide a fairer comparison of performance when training on STARC-9 compared to NCT and HMU, we performed additional validation of the best-performing model trained on each of these three datasets on an external TCGA-CRC dataset (please see Sections 4.1 and 4.2 for results).\
In addition, to showcase the generalizability of the model trained on STARC-9, we curated a small test set of the seven common tissue classes from the IMP‑CRS10K dataset [42] using ten WSIs. In total, 1,093 image tiles were annotated for validating the performance of the models. The corresponding evaluation results are presented in Table 3. STARC‑9–trained model achieves 95.55% F1‑macro and 96.61% accuracy, consistently outperforming the HMU and NCT–trained models, reflecting STARC‑9’s diverse tissue diversity and representative samples that improve generalization on external validation sets.\
\

|---------------------|--------------------|--------------------|------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|-------------------------|
| IMP-CRS10K [42]  | 45.85| 62.46| 95.55| 69.62| 76.40| 96.61  |

These were the only practical options available to us, as we were unfortunately unable to find any additional publicly available CRC benchmark datasets containing the precise tissue type classes and accurate, pathologist-validated annotations that could be used for external validation. Given the significant time and effort required to acquire additional external validation datasets from other institutions (requiring IRB, data sharing agreements, and other institutional approvals, as well as recruitment of subspecialty pathologists to perform dataset annotation), we were unable to include additional institutional validation datasets in time for this submission.  
[42] Neto, P. C., et al. (2024). IMP Whole-Slide Images of Colorectal Samples 2024 [Data set]. INESC TEC.   \
\
**4.The experiments should be further enriched by:\
(i) TransNeXt (CVPR2024) and OverLoCK (CVPR2025).\
(ii) Masked image modeling and contrastive learning-based pretraining.**\

**1.In Section 1, the paper states that 630,000 sampled images were validated by pathologists for tissue classification accuracy. However, this raises questions about whether this aligns with the claim in the introduction regarding the "limited manual review." This assertion lacks further clarification or comparative explanation.**\
Thank you for the opportunity to clarify. We realize that the use of "minimal" to describe the manual review (line 94 in the original version of the manuscript) was not the best word choice. Rather than minimizing the need for manual review (which we feel will continue to remain an important final step when creating a high-quality labeled dataset for applications in healthcare) it would be more accurate to state that our approach significantly reduces the manual burden of annotation and tile selection, compared to the conventional approach to constructing tissue-type classification datasets (which involves manual pathologist delineation of regions of interest (ROI) within a WSI, followed by extraction of tiles from these ROIs). In contrast, with our automated DeepCluster++ framework, once the tiles have been collected for each tissue class within a WSI (which would normally require a significant amount of human time and effort using the conventional manual approach), a pathologist can simply use QuPath software to re-map the collected tiles back onto the original WSI from which they were taken, then confirm through a quick WSI-level visual inspection that the tiles for each tissue class were correctly assigned by DeepCluster++. This quality‐control pass takes less than five minutes per slide, which is significantly less time than would be required to perform manual ROI annotation for each tissue class (following the conventional annotation and tile selection approach). By restricting the pathologist's workload to this final WSI-level verification step, our DeepCluster++ allows for the collection of tissue-type specific datasets with high‐confidence labels and significantly reduced manual effort. We will revise the wording in our final manuscript to clarify this important point and avoid misinterpretation. \
\
**2.Figure 2 lacks clarity, as it is difficult to locate image 48 mentioned in Section 3.3 of the paper. The current presentation of the figure is not user-friendly and hinders effective viewing.**\
We apologize for the lack of clarity in Figure 2. In the revised manuscript, we will replace it with a higher‑resolution version, enlarge panel 2(b), and clearly annotate cluster indices, especially highlighting cluster 48 as referenced in Section 3.3. We will also update the caption to guide readers directly to the relevant subpanel and include call‑outs to improve readability.\
\
**3.In Section 3.1, the paper introduces the training of the AE_CRC model but lacks a clear explanation of the category distribution for the 100,000 256×256-pixel patches containing tumor and normal samples. This omission makes the description insufficiently clear.**\
Thank you for this feedback. To train our AutoEncoder, we selected 5 tumor and 5 normal WSIs, covering all nine histological tissue types. These WSIs were drawn from a set entirely separate from our STARC-9 training and validation sets. After standard preprocessing, we randomly sampled 100,000 256x256 tiles for training AutoEncoder and ensured robust reconstruction of the full spectrum of colorectal histology. We will expand Section 3.1 in the final manuscript to include these details. \
\
**4.In Section 4, there is a significant discrepancy in the sizes of the STARC-9, NCT, and HMU datasets. However, the paper employs identical training configurations across all three datasets. This uniform setting fails to account for the inherent differences in dataset scale and distribution, making it difficult to convincingly demonstrate the claimed superiority or advantages of any particular dataset.**\
We agree with your observation that there is a discrepancy in the dataset sizes between STARC-9, NCT, and HMU. However, we feel that maintaining identical training configurations, including batch size and optimizer settings, across datasets is important for a fair and unbiased model comparison. As our primary objective was to isolate the impact of the dataset on model performance, we kept the training configurations consistent to avoid possible confounding introduced by different hyperparameters being applied to the datasets. In addition, a consistent batch size ensured uniform model updates, with the same number of samples processed per iteration regardless of dataset scale. This standardization avoids a biased performance evaluation which might arise if tailoring configurations to each dataset. \
\
**5.The tumor tissue segmentation experiment uses only two 2048×2048 images, which is insufficient to convincingly demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The evidence provided is too limited to support the conclusions. More samples are needed for a reliable evaluation.** \
In the current manuscript, our primary objective was to collect a dataset for multi-class tissue-type classification, and the inclusion of the experimental results on the segmentation task was more exploratory, as we were interested in assessing the utility of STARC-9 for training of downstream segmentation models, especially for the TUM tissue type. We completely agree that two 2048×2048 patches alone are insufficient to draw any firm conclusions regarding segmentation performance. Unfortunately, no publicly available CRC WSI repositories came with readily usable, high‑quality TUM masks for a larger scale experiment, and existing weakly‑supervised tools did not provide the precision required for generating tissue segmentation masks. \
However, acknowledging the reviewers concern in this regard, we have now prepared a test set by enlisting expert pathologists to manually annotate (ground truth) the TUM region in the patches of size 2048×2048. We selected 45 patches (3 per slide) from 15 Stanford WSIs and 50 patches (2 per slide) from 25 TCGA-CRC WSIs, which are fully independent of our training and validation sets. Table 6 reports Intersection-over-Union (IoU) and Dice scores for tumor segmentation on these held-out sets. Moreover, STARC-9-trained models exhibited substantially narrower standard deviations in both IoU and Dice scores, demonstrating more consistent and robust tumor delineation across diverse samples. This expanded evaluation confirms that the performance gains afforded by STARC-9 generalize to a larger, more heterogeneous cohort. We will include this analysis in the final version of the manuscript.

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding cross‑validation. In the current context, generating multi-fold cross-validation splits for training and testing from the collection of 630,000 tiles would potentially result in the inclusion of tiles from the same WSI across training and test splits, introducing bias in the downstream performance evaluation. This might be avoided by performing WSI‑level k‑fold splits instead, but this process would be complicated by the inherent imbalance in the WSI-level distribution of tile counts for each tissue type class within the dataset, as some WSI contain fewer examples of certain tissue classes (especially the LYM, NCS, and BLD classes), making the generation of evenly-stratified folds nearly impossible. Instead, to ensure an independent evaluation, we instead opted to reserve an entire held‑out set of WSIs from our institution for validation, and also performed validation on an external TCGA-CRC dataset. This approach ensured that the observed performance metrics better reflected model generalization ability across distinct WSI, while avoiding the pitfall represented by imbalanced/underrepresented tissue classes within individual cross‑validation folds.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors present STARC-9, a large-scale dataset of 630,000 histopathological image tiles, uniformly sampled across nine clinically relevant tissue classes for colorectal cancer. This dataset is constructed using a novel semi-automated pipeline called DeepCluster++, which combines domain-specific autoencoder feature extraction, K-means clustering, and equal-frequency binning, followed by expert pathologist validation. The authors compare STARC-9 with two leading public datasets (NCT-CRC-HE-100K and HMU-GC-HE-30K) on a wide range of classification models (CNNs, transformers, pathology-specific foundation models). The results suggest clear improvements in classification accuracy, generalizability, and segmentation quality.

- The paper is clear and well-organized, making it easy to understand.
- The proposed dataset is very substantial and benefits the community.
- The proposed dataset provides 9 classes of tissues with 70000 examples for each. This address the problem of class imbalance and morphological diversity.
- The proposed pipeline, DeepCluster++ is interesting and allow to minimize manual effort and maximizes intra-class variation.
- Many existing models are benchmarked
- The experimental evaluation alos provide some visualizations facilitating interpretability for the reader

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Details on patient distribution are lacking in the dataset.
- Much of the evaluation of the proposed dataset is carried out using validation sets from the same center, which may bias the results.
- The limitations of the paper are barely discussed.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Data and code are available. Code could be better documented to facilitate reproducibility of experiments.

additional_feedback.value:
- It would be interesting to mention the distribution of patients in the final version of STARC-9 (among the 200 initially planned). Is the number of tiles per patient balanced?
- It is unclear whether the WSIs used to train the AutoEncoder are the same as the tiles ultimately used in STARC-9. If so, doesn't this introduce bias? Especially since the features considered for clustering come from a CNN, doesn't this bias the analysis of various state-of-the-art methods (including CNNs)?
- In Section 3.3, it is unclear how tissue classes are identified and associated with tiles? The autoencoder is unsupervised.
- Since the validation sets come from the same center, do they include the same patients? 
- The authors observe a real performance gain on their validation sets when trained on STARC-9 compared to NCT and HMU. I wonder if the fact that the datasets come from the same center does not partly explain such a difference? It could be interesting to evaluate the performance of the models trained on STARC-9 and evaluated on NCT and HMU, in order to analyze the generalizability.

The authors have addressed most of my concerns/questions with substantial and detailed responses.
My positive assessment of the paper is therefore confirmed and remains fully valid

summary.value:
The paper introduces STARC-9, a large-scale dataset designed for multi-class tissue-type classification in colorectal cancer histopathology images. The authors identify key limitations in existing datasets (insufficient morphological diversity, class imbalance, and low quality images), and propose STARC-9 to address them. 
To build the dataset, they also propose DeepCluster++, a semi-automated approach consisting of three steps: (1) feature extraction via a trained an encoder, (2) clustering followed by equal-frequency binning for sampling diverse tiles, and (3) expert pathologist verification. 
Finally, the paper validates the utility of STARC-9 by showing that models trained on it outperform those trained on existing datasets.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper is well-written and organized, and it is easy to follow. 

With this dataset, the authors address the lack of high-quality public datasets for colorectal cancer classification. This dataset is valuable for the community and can foster future research and development of clinical tools. 

The proposed methodology, DeepCluster++, effectively reduces the manual labeling requirements by limiting pathologist involvement to a verification step on carefully pre-selected tiles. 

The proposed dataset is validated using a wide variety of vision models (up to 17 as per Table 1), including pathology foundation models. The experimental results are consistent and show significant improvements in classification and segmentation generalization compared to existing CRC datasets. 

Finally, the dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face, promoting reproducibility and adoption.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**The DeepCluster++ methodology.** My main concern is related to the DeepCluster++ methodology. The authors do not review or compare similar existing dataset construction methods from digital pathology or related fields. A natural question is why the existing methodologies are not enough to build the STARC-9 dataset. I believe that including such a discussion would strengthen the paper
Additionally, some design choices within DeepCluster++ appear somewhat arbitrary. While the experimental results demonstrate the framework’s utility, the lack of rationale for key decisions (e.g., specific hyperparameters, sampling strategy) undermines the method’s credibility. I acknowledge that a full ablation study on the entire dataset is infeasible. I suggest performing targeted ablations on a smaller-scale subset, so that the importance of each component is clarified. 
Some specific aspects that could be improved are:
- Why was an autoencoder chosen for feature extraction rather than leveraging existing pathology foundation models, which might provide richer, more informative feature spaces to enhance clustering and sampling?
- How to choose the different hyperparameters? Number of examples per cluster, number of distance-based groups, percentage of tiles to sample from each bin… How do they affect the quality of the dataset?

**Formatting errors.** There are some errors in the text that correspond to incorrect formatting of Latex equations (see, for example, section 3.2). 

**Lack of clarity in tables.** Tables are not presented with sufficient clarity. It is difficult to understand them.
- In Table 1, the meaning of the text in bold is not explained. 
- In Table 2, it is unclear whether the results correspond to the same model. Second row shows performance values that do not match any entry in Table 1, causing potential confusion. I think it is misleading not to clarify which model corresponds to each cell. 

**Bias and fairness.** The paper does not discuss patient demographics (e.g., nationality, sex) or analyze potential biases related to these factors. The justification in the NeurIPS Paper Checklist related to this matter is missing (point 9. Code of ethics).

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: The paper does not discuss patient demographics (e.g., nationality, sex) or analyze potential biases related to these factors. The justification in the NeurIPS Paper Checklist related to this matter is missing (point 9. Code of ethics).

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors have released the dataset through Huggingface Datasets (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Path2AI/STARC-9/tree/main), as well as the weights corresponding to the models used in the empirical evaluation. The code corresponding to the DeepCluster++ methodology and the code to train and evaluate the models are in the provided Github repository (https://github.com/Path2AI/STARC-9)

additional_feedback.value: I believe this paper and the STARC-9 dataset represent a valuable contribution to the community. Addressing the limitations above would strengthen the work and its impact. I highly encourage the authors to address them.

final_justification.value:
The authors have written a high-quality rebuttal, addressing most of my concerns. One minor issue is that the ablation study only explores variations in the cluster size, without examining the impact of the number of bins or the sampling percentage. Nevertheless, given the limited time available for the rebuttal, I find it to be sufficient.

After reading the discussions prompted by other reviewers' comments, I believe that the work has improved significantly. I have updated my rating from 3 to 5.

summary.value: This paper introduces STARC-9, a large-scale dataset for multi-class tissue classification in colorectal cancer (CRC) histopathology. The authors propose a DeepCluster++ framework, which converts whole-slide images (WSIs) into image tiles, thereby constructing a large dataset comprising 630,000 images. The experiments primarily focus on multi-label classification, evaluating the performance of various models on this task.

strengths_contributions.value:
The proposed STARC-9 dataset is not only large-scale but also highly meaningful for multi-class tissue classification in CRC histopathology, providing a valuable resource for researchers in this field.

The DeepCluster++ framework presented in this paper exhibits versatility and has the potential to be applied to other medical domains, suggesting a broader impact beyond CRC histopathology.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I have several concerns regarding this paper, specifically with regards to the dataset construction and experimental sections:

1. The use of unsupervised autoencoders in DeepCluster++ to extract latent features for clustering is an interesting approach, but it raises concerns about whether the autoencoder can accurately capture image-level semantic information, which is crucial for precise dataset construction. If the feature embedding learned by the autoencoder is inaccurate, it will significantly impact the subsequent steps and affect the reliability of the dataset. The authors should conduct further analysis, such as statistical analysis and visualization, to address this concern.

2. The statement "Finally, the selected tiles are verified by expert gastrointestinal pathologists to ensure classification accuracy" raises questions about whether all 630,000 images were reviewed by experts. If only a few samples are reviewed, this could be problematic in the medical field, as incorrect data can lead to biased models that affect clinical use. Additionally, the authors should provide information about the qualifications and experience of the pathologists involved in the review process to ensure the dataset's review process is reliable.

3. The performance of different models on the STARC-9 training set is surprisingly high, with even a simple ConvNet trained from scratch achieving an F1 score of 97.93 in Table 1. Given the large size of the training dataset, this raises concerns about the dataset's distribution and potential leakage of the STANFORD-CRC-HE-VAL dataset into the training data. I suggest using some public validation sets to mitigate this concern.

4. The experiments should be further enriched by: 
- Using more advanced vision models, such as TransNeXt (CVPR2024) and OverLoCK (CVPR2025), as the mentioned SOTA models are outdated.
- Conducting experiments using masked image modeling and contrastive learning-based pretraining, which could be an interesting approach given the large size of the proposed dataset.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel large-scale, high-quality dataset, STARC-9, designed for multi-class tissue classification in colorectal cancer histopathology. The dataset effectively addresses critical issues such as class imbalance and lack of diversity, which are prevalent in existing colorectal cancer datasets. Additionally, the study introduces the DeepCluster++ framework, which leverages a combination of unsupervised feature extraction, clustering, and equal-frequency binning techniques to efficiently generate training samples from whole slide images (WSIs).

strengths_contributions.value:

title.value: STARC-9: A Large-scale Dataset for Multi-Class Tissue Classification for CRC Histopathology

abstract.value: Multi-class tissue-type classification of colorectal cancer (CRC) histopathologic images is a significant step in the development of downstream machine learning models for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, publicly available CRC datasets used to build tissue classifiers often suffer from insufficient morphologic diversity, class imbalance, and low-quality image tiles, limiting downstream model performance and generalizability. To address this research gap, we introduce STARC-9 (STAnford coloRectal Cancer), a large-scale dataset for multi-class tissue classification. STARC-9 comprises 630,000 histopathologic image tiles uniformly sampled across nine clinically relevant tissue classes (each represented by 70,000 tiles), systematically extracted from hematoxylin & eosin-stained whole-slide images (WSI) from 200 CRC patients at the Stanford University School of Medicine. To construct STARC-9, we propose a novel framework, DeepCluster++, consisting of two primary steps to ensure diversity within each tissue class, followed by pathologist verification. First, an encoder from an autoencoder trained specifically on histopathologic images is used to extract feature vectors from all tiles within a given input WSI. Next, K-means clustering groups morphologically similar tiles, followed by an equal-frequency binning method to sample diverse patterns within each tissue class. Finally, the selected tiles are verified by expert gastrointestinal pathologists to ensure classification accuracy. This semi-automated approach significantly reduces the manual effort required for dataset curation while producing high-quality training examples. To validate the utility of STARC-9, we benchmarked baseline convolutional neural networks, transformers, and pathology-specific foundation models on downstream multi-class CRC tissue classification and segmentation tasks when trained on STARC-9 versus publicly available datasets, demonstrating superior generalizability of models trained on STARC-9. Although we demonstrate the utility of DeepCluster++ on CRC as a pilot use-case, it is a flexible framework that can be used for constructing high-quality datasets from large WSI repositories across a wide range of cancer and non-cancer applications.
